MATH_001.name: Set
description: A **set** is a _well-defined_ collection of **distinct objects**, known as **elements**.
Sets are usually denoted by **capital letters** with elements inside curly braces, e.g., $A = \{a, b, c\}$.
The **order** of elements does _not_ matter, and **duplicate elements** are ignored.
MATH_001.notes: Think of a set as a bag of unique items. It's the **fundamental building block** for nearly all of mathematics!
references: Halmos, P. R. (1960). Naive Set Theory

MATH_002.name: Subset
description: A set $A$ is a **subset** of a set $B$ if _every element_ of $A$ is also an element of $B$.
This relationship is denoted as $A \subseteq B$.
**Every set is a subset of itself.**
MATH_002.notes: If set $B$ contains _all_ the items of set $A$ (and possibly more), then $A$ is a **subset** of $B$. Easy peasy!

MATH_003.name: Empty Set
description: The **empty set** is the _unique_ set that contains **no elements**.
It is denoted by $\emptyset$ or $\{\}$.
The empty set is a **subset of every set**.
MATH_003.notes: It might seem strange, but the concept of _'nothing'_ is **incredibly important** for defining everything else.

MATH_004.name: Cartesian Product
description: The **Cartesian product** of two sets $A$ and $B$ is the set of all **ordered pairs** $(a, b)$ where $a \in A$ and $b \in B$.
It is denoted by $A \times B$.
This concept extends to _more than two sets_, forming **n-tuples**.
MATH_004.notes: If you have a set of shirts and a set of pants, the Cartesian product is **all possible outfits**!

MATH_005.name: Power Set
description: The **power set** of a set $S$ is the set of _all possible subsets_ of $S$, including the empty set and $S$ itself.
It is denoted by $P(S)$ or $2^S$.
If $S$ has $n$ elements, its power set $P(S)$ has **$2^n$ elements**.
MATH_005.notes: The power set reveals the **complete substructure** of a set. It's a _'set of sets'_!

MATH_006.name: Mapping (Function)
description: A **mapping** (or **function**) $f$ from a set $A$ to a set $B$ is a _rule_ that assigns to each element $x \in A$ **exactly one** element $y \in B$.
$A$ is called the **domain**, and $B$ is the **codomain**.
This is denoted as $f: A \to B$.
MATH_006.notes: Mappings are the **action heroes** of math, describing _relationships_ and _transformations_ between sets.

MATH_007.name: Injective Mapping
description: An **injective** (or **one-to-one**) mapping ensures that _no two elements_ in the domain map to the same element in the codomain.
Think of it as a **'no sharing outputs'** rule.
MATH_007.notes: Injective functions **preserve distinctness**. They don't _merge_ or _lose_ information.

MATH_008.name: Surjective Mapping
description: A **surjective** (or **onto**) mapping ensures that _every element_ in the codomain $B$ has **at least one** corresponding element in the domain $A$.
The **range** of the function is _equal to_ its **codomain**.
Think of it as **'covering all the targets'**.
MATH_008.notes: Surjective functions **hit every possible output value**. _Nothing_ in the codomain is left out.

MATH_009.name: Bijective Mapping
description: A **bijective** mapping is _both_ **injective** _and_ **surjective**.
It creates a **perfect one-to-one correspondence** between the elements of the domain and the codomain.
Bijective functions have a **unique inverse function**.
MATH_009.notes: Bijections are the **gold standard** of mappings, showing that two sets are _structurally identical_ in size.

MATH_010.name: Category
description: A **category** is a collection of **'objects'** and **'morphisms'** (arrows) between them.
It includes an _associative_ **composition** of morphisms and an **identity morphism** for each object.
**Category theory** is a _high-level abstraction_ that studies mathematical structures and their relationships.
MATH_010.notes: This is **math about math**! It unifies concepts from different fields by focusing on _structure_ and _transformations_.
references: Mac Lane, S. (1998). Categories for the Working Mathematician

MATH_011.name: Isomorphism
description: In category theory, an **isomorphism** is a morphism $f: A \to B$ that has a **two-sided inverse** $g: B \to A$.
This means $f \circ g = 1_B$ and $g \circ f = 1_A$.
**Isomorphic objects** are _structurally identical_ from the perspective of the category.
MATH_011.notes: This is the **categorical generalization** of a bijection. It's the _ultimate_ **'sameness' detector**.

MATH_012.name: Monomorphism
description: A **monomorphism** (or **mono**) is the _categorical generalization_ of an **injective mapping**.
It is a **'left-cancelable'** morphism: if $f \circ g_1 = f \circ g_2$, then $g_1 = g_2$.
In the category of sets, monomorphisms are _exactly_ the **injective functions**.
MATH_012.notes: While it feels like injectivity, this definition works in contexts where _'elements' don't exist_!

MATH_013.name: Epimorphism
description: An **epimorphism** (or **epi**) is the _categorical generalization_ of a **surjective mapping**.
It is a **'right-cancelable'** morphism: if $g_1 \circ f = g_2 \circ f$, then $g_1 = g_2$.
In the category of sets, epimorphisms are _exactly_ the **surjective functions**.
MATH_013.notes: **Beware!** In some categories (like **Rings**), an epimorphism is _not always_ surjective. Abstraction is tricky!

MATH_014.name: Functor
description: A **functor** is a _mapping between categories_.
It maps **objects** to **objects** and **morphisms** to **morphisms** in a way that _preserves_ **composition** and **identity**.
Functors are the **'morphisms' of categories**, allowing us to compare them.
MATH_014.notes: If categories are _worlds_ of mathematical structures, functors are the **portals** between them.

MATH_015.name: Number Theory
description: **Number theory** is a branch of _pure mathematics_ devoted primarily to the study of the **integers** and **integer-valued functions**.
It explores properties like **divisibility**, **prime numbers**, and solutions to **equations in integers**.
MATH_015.notes: The **'Queen of Mathematics'**! It's full of _simple-to-state_ problems that are **incredibly hard** to solve.
references: Hardy, G. H., & Wright, E. M. (1938). An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers

MATH_016.name: Rational & Irrational Numbers
description: A **rational number** can be expressed as a fraction $\frac{p}{q}$ of two integers, where $q \neq 0$.
An **irrational number** _cannot_ be expressed as such a fraction. Its decimal representation _never terminates_ and _never repeats_.
Examples of irrationals include $\sqrt{2}$, $\pi$, and $e$.
MATH_016.notes: The discovery of **irrational numbers** was a _major shock_ to the ancient Greeks, who believed _all numbers_ were rational!

MATH_017.name: Proof by Contradiction
description: A method of **indirect proof** where one assumes the _opposite_ of what they want to prove.
You then follow a series of **logical steps** until you arrive at a _logically impossible_ conclusion (a **contradiction**).
This proves that the **initial assumption** must have been _false_.
MATH_017.notes: A **powerful** and sometimes _sneaky_ way to prove something is true by showing its opposite is **absurd**.

MATH_018.name: Pythagorean Theorem
description: In a **right-angled triangle**, the _square of the length_ of the **hypotenuse** (the side opposite the right angle) is equal to the **sum of the squares** of the other two sides.
The formula is $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.
MATH_018.notes: One of the **most famous** and **most useful** theorems in all of geometry!

versions.description: This exercise tests your ability to combine _algebraic manipulation_ with a **proof by contradiction**.
versions.hints: Assume the expression equals a rational number $r$. **Square both sides** and try to isolate a single square root term.
versions.result: Assume $\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3} = r$ (rational). Squaring gives $5 + 2\sqrt{6} = r^2$, which means $\sqrt{6} = \frac{r^2 - 5}{2}$. Since $r$ is rational, the right side is rational, implying $\sqrt{6}$ is rational. This is a **known contradiction**. Thus, the original assumption is _false_.

versions.description: Similar to the previous version, but with different numbers. This reinforces the _general technique_ for proving irrationality of sums of radicals.
versions.hints: Follow the same approach: assume $\sqrt{5} + \sqrt{7} = r$ (rational), then **square both sides**.
versions.result: Assume $\sqrt{5} + \sqrt{7} = r$ (rational). Squaring: $(\sqrt{5} + \sqrt{7})^2 = r^2$ gives $5 + 2\sqrt{35} + 7 = r^2$, so $12 + 2\sqrt{35} = r^2$. Thus $\sqrt{35} = \frac{r^2 - 12}{2}$. Since $r$ is rational, this implies $\sqrt{35}$ is rational, a **contradiction**.

versions.description: A _variation_ with **subtraction** instead of addition. The technique remains similar.
versions.hints: Assume $\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2} = r$ (rational). Square both sides and isolate the radical term.
versions.result: Assume $\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2} = r$ (rational). Squaring: $(\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2})^2 = r^2$ gives $3 - 2\sqrt{6} + 2 = r^2$, so $5 - 2\sqrt{6} = r^2$. Thus $\sqrt{6} = \frac{5 - r^2}{2}$. Since $r$ is rational, this implies $\sqrt{6}$ is rational, a **contradiction**.

versions.description: This **classic proof** uses the _definition of logarithms_ and the **fundamental theorem of arithmetic**.
versions.hints: Assume $\log_2 3 = \frac{p}{q}$. Rewrite this in **exponential form** and look for a contradiction related to _prime factors_.
versions.result: Assume $\log_2 3 = \frac{p}{q}$. This means $2^{p/q} = 3$, so $2^p = 3^q$. By the **unique prime factorization theorem**, an integer power of $2$ cannot equal an integer power of $3$ (unless both exponents are $0$, which is _not_ the case). This is a **contradiction**.

versions.description: A similar problem with _different bases_. This reinforces understanding of the **fundamental theorem of arithmetic**.
versions.hints: Assume $\log_3 5 = \frac{p}{q}$, which means $3^{p/q} = 5$. Convert to integer powers.
versions.result: Assume $\log_3 5 = \frac{p}{q}$. This means $3^{p/q} = 5$, so $3^p = 5^q$. By **unique prime factorization**, an integer power of $3$ cannot equal an integer power of $5$. This is a **contradiction**.

versions.description: Another variation using _base 10_, which many students find more intuitive.
versions.hints: Assume $\log_{10} 2 = \frac{p}{q}$. This means $10^{p/q} = 2$. What does this imply about prime factorizations?
versions.result: Assume $\log_{10} 2 = \frac{p}{q}$. This means $10^{p/q} = 2$, so $10^p = 2^q$. Since $10 = 2 \times 5$, we have $(2 \times 5)^p = 2^q$, which gives $2^p \times 5^p = 2^q$. This would require $5^p = 2^{q-p}$, but by **unique prime factorization**, a power of $5$ cannot equal a power of $2$. **Contradiction**.

versions.description: This exercise requires a **geometric proof** to demonstrate the famous relationship in a _right-angled triangle_.
versions.hints: Consider a large square with side length $(a+b)$. Arrange **four copies** of the triangle inside it. What shape is left in the _middle_?
versions.result: Arrange four right triangles (sides $a$, $b$, $c$) inside a square of side $(a+b)$. The **total area** is $(a+b)^2$. The area is also the sum of the four triangles $4 \times \frac{1}{2}ab$ plus the area of the inner square, $c^2$. Equating them: $a^2 + 2ab + b^2 = 2ab + c^2$, which simplifies to $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.

versions.statement: Prove the Pythagorean theorem using **similar triangles**.
versions.description: An _alternative proof_ using the concept of **similarity** in geometry.
versions.hints: Drop a perpendicular from the right angle to the hypotenuse. This creates **three similar triangles**.
versions.result: In a right triangle with sides $a$, $b$, and hypotenuse $c$, drop a perpendicular from the right angle to the hypotenuse, creating segments $p$ and $q$ where $p + q = c$. The three triangles (original and two smaller ones) are **similar**. From similarity ratios: $\frac{a}{c} = \frac{p}{a}$ and $\frac{b}{c} = \frac{q}{b}$. This gives $a^2 = cp$ and $b^2 = cq$. Adding: $a^2 + b^2 = cp + cq = c(p+q) = c^2$.

versions.statement: Verify the Pythagorean theorem for a **3-4-5 triangle** by calculation.
versions.description: A _concrete numerical example_ that demonstrates the theorem with specific values.
versions.hints: Simply substitute $a = 3$, $b = 4$, $c = 5$ into the formula $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.
versions.result: For a triangle with sides $a = 3$, $b = 4$, and $c = 5$: Calculate $a^2 + b^2 = 3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25$. Calculate $c^2 = 5^2 = 25$. Since $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, the **Pythagorean theorem holds** for this triangle.
